cookieless-analytics.title: What is Cookieless analytics? - Glossary | Ciphera
cookieless-analytics.description: Cookieless analytics measures website traffic without setting cookies or any other persistent client-side identifier — counts are derived from request-level signals, not a stored ID that follows a browser over time.

third-party-cookies.title: What is Third-party cookies? - Glossary | Ciphera
third-party-cookies.description: A third-party cookie is set by a domain other than the one the user is visiting — typically an ad or analytics vendor embedded via script — letting that vendor recognize the same browser across unrelated sites.

fingerprinting.title: What is Browser fingerprinting? - Glossary | Ciphera
fingerprinting.description: Browser fingerprinting identifies a device by combining device and browser attributes — screen size, installed fonts, GPU details, timezone, and more — into a composite signature, without storing anything on the device.

tracking-pixel.title: What is Tracking pixel? - Glossary | Ciphera
tracking-pixel.description: A tracking pixel is a tiny, invisible image embedded in a page or email whose load request signals to the hosting server that the content was opened, along with the viewer’s IP and client details.

bounce-rate.title: What is Bounce rate? - Glossary | Ciphera
bounce-rate.description: Bounce rate is the share of visits in which a user views a single page and leaves without any further interaction or navigation — a rough signal of whether a landing page held attention.

unique-visitors.title: What is Unique visitors? - Glossary | Ciphera
unique-visitors.description: Unique visitors counts distinct people (or devices) visiting a site over a period, as opposed to pageviews, which counts every page load — the same visitor loading ten pages is one unique visitor and ten pageviews.

session.title: What is Session (analytics)? - Glossary | Ciphera
session.description: In web analytics, a session is a group of interactions — pageviews, events — from one visitor treated as a single continuous visit, typically closed out after a period of inactivity (commonly 30 minutes).

referrer.title: What is Referrer? - Glossary | Ciphera
referrer.description: The referrer is the URL of the page a visitor was on immediately before arriving at the current one, sent by the browser in the HTTP Referer header (or omitted, per the page’s referrer policy).

utm-parameters.title: What is UTM parameters? - Glossary | Ciphera
utm-parameters.description: UTM parameters are standardized query-string tags (utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign, and related fields) appended to a URL so analytics tools can attribute traffic to a specific campaign, channel, or link.

do-not-track.title: What is Do Not Track (DNT)? - Glossary | Ciphera
do-not-track.description: Do Not Track was an HTTP header and browser setting, standardized as DNT, that signaled a user’s preference not to be tracked across sites — largely abandoned because sites were never legally required to honor it.
do-not-track.ogtitle: What is Do Not Track (DNT)? | Ciphera

global-privacy-control.title: What is Global Privacy Control (GPC)? - Glossary | Ciphera
global-privacy-control.description: Global Privacy Control is a browser-sent HTTP signal (Sec-GPC: 1) expressing a user’s opt-out of sale and sharing of personal data — legally binding in California and other US states, unlike Do Not Track.
global-privacy-control.ogtitle: What is Global Privacy Control (GPC)? | Ciphera

opaque.title: What is OPAQUE? - Glossary | Ciphera
opaque.description: OPAQUE is an asymmetric password-authenticated key exchange (aPAKE) protocol, standardized in RFC 9807, that lets a server verify a password without ever seeing it — the password never leaves the client, even during registration.

pake.title: What is PAKE (password-authenticated key exchange)? - Glossary | Ciphera
pake.description: A PAKE is a cryptographic protocol in which two parties use a shared password to establish a strong session key — without ever transmitting the password or exposing it to offline guessing from intercepted traffic.
pake.ogtitle: What is PAKE (password-authenticated key exchange)? | Ciphera

oprf.title: What is OPRF (oblivious pseudorandom function)? - Glossary | Ciphera
oprf.description: An OPRF is a two-party protocol where a server holding a secret key helps a client evaluate a pseudorandom function on the client’s input — without the server learning the input or the output, and without the client learning the key.
oprf.ogtitle: What is OPRF (oblivious pseudorandom function)? | Ciphera

zero-knowledge.title: What is Zero-knowledge? - Glossary | Ciphera
zero-knowledge.description: In applied privacy engineering, zero-knowledge describes systems designed so the service operator cannot read user data or secrets — verification and storage work without the server ever holding the plaintext.

zero-knowledge-authentication.title: What is Zero-knowledge authentication? - Glossary | Ciphera
zero-knowledge-authentication.description: Authentication in which the server verifies you know your password without ever receiving it — during signup or login, in any form. The standard construction today is an aPAKE such as OPAQUE (RFC 9807).

blind-index.title: What is Blind index? - Glossary | Ciphera
blind-index.description: A blind index is a keyed, deterministic hash of a field (such as an email address) stored in place of the plaintext, so a database can look records up by exact match without holding — or leaking — the value itself.

key-stretching.title: What is Key stretching? - Glossary | Ciphera
key-stretching.description: Key stretching turns a low-entropy secret like a password into a stronger key by making each derivation deliberately expensive — thousands to millions of iterations, or memory-hard computation — so brute-force guessing becomes uneconomical.

argon2id.title: What is Argon2id? - Glossary | Ciphera
argon2id.description: Argon2id is the recommended variant of Argon2, winner of the Password Hashing Competition: a memory-hard key-derivation function that makes password guessing expensive on GPUs and custom hardware, while resisting side-channel attacks.

hkdf.title: What is HKDF? - Glossary | Ciphera
hkdf.description: HKDF (HMAC-based key derivation function, RFC 5869) expands one strong secret into any number of independent, purpose-bound keys via extract-then-expand — the standard way to turn a shared secret into separate encryption, signing, and session keys.

end-to-end-encryption.title: What is End-to-end encryption (E2EE)? - Glossary | Ciphera
end-to-end-encryption.description: End-to-end encryption means data is encrypted on the sender’s device and decrypted only on the recipient’s — every intermediary, including the service operator, handles ciphertext it cannot read.

aes-256-gcm.title: What is AES-256-GCM? - Glossary | Ciphera
aes-256-gcm.description: AES-256-GCM is authenticated encryption: the AES block cipher with 256-bit keys in Galois/Counter Mode, providing confidentiality and integrity in one pass — tampered ciphertext fails authentication instead of decrypting to garbage.

passkeys.title: What is Passkeys (WebAuthn / FIDO2)? - Glossary | Ciphera
passkeys.description: Passkeys are public-key login credentials based on the FIDO2/WebAuthn standards: your device holds a private key and signs a per-site challenge, so there is no shared secret to phish, leak, or reuse across sites.

pkce.title: What is PKCE? - Glossary | Ciphera
pkce.description: PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange, RFC 7636) hardens the OAuth 2.0 authorization-code flow: the client commits to a one-time secret up front, so an intercepted authorization code is useless without it.

jwt.title: What is JWT (JSON Web Token)? - Glossary | Ciphera
jwt.description: A JWT is a compact, signed token carrying claims (user ID, expiry, scopes) that services can verify statelessly — any holder of the verification key can check authenticity without a database lookup.
jwt.ogtitle: What is JWT (JSON Web Token)? | Ciphera

totp.title: What is TOTP (time-based one-time password)? - Glossary | Ciphera
totp.description: TOTP (RFC 6238) generates six-digit codes from a shared secret and the current time, giving accounts a second factor that changes every 30 seconds and works fully offline in any authenticator app.
totp.ogtitle: What is TOTP (time-based one-time password)? | Ciphera

srp.title: What is SRP (Secure Remote Password)? - Glossary | Ciphera
srp.description: SRP is a 1990s password-authenticated key exchange that lets clients log in without sending the password. It was the workhorse aPAKE for two decades and is now superseded by OPAQUE (RFC 9807).
srp.ogtitle: What is SRP (Secure Remote Password)? | Ciphera

transactional-email.title: What is Transactional email? - Glossary | Ciphera
transactional-email.description: Transactional email is a message triggered by a specific user action or system event — password resets, receipts, verification codes, shipping notices — as opposed to marketing email sent to a list on a schedule.

dkim.title: What is DKIM? - Glossary | Ciphera
dkim.description: DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail, RFC 6376) lets a sending domain cryptographically sign outgoing email — a public key published in DNS verifies the signature, proving headers and body were not altered in transit.

spf.title: What is SPF? - Glossary | Ciphera
spf.description: SPF (Sender Policy Framework, RFC 7208) is a DNS TXT record listing which mail servers may send email for a domain — receiving servers check the connecting IP against it to catch spoofed sender addresses.

dmarc.title: What is DMARC? - Glossary | Ciphera
dmarc.description: DMARC (RFC 7489) is a DNS policy record tying SPF and DKIM together: it requires one to align with the visible From address, tells receivers what to do on failure, and requests reporting on the results.

mta-sts.title: What is MTA-STS? - Glossary | Ciphera
mta-sts.description: MTA-STS (RFC 8461) lets a domain require TLS for all inbound email delivery, published and fetched over HTTPS rather than trusted opportunistically — closing the downgrade attack that plain SMTP TLS leaves open.

open-tracking.title: What is Email open tracking? - Glossary | Ciphera
open-tracking.description: Email open tracking records when a recipient views a message, typically via an embedded tracking pixel that silently reports back to the sender the moment the email client loads remote images.
open-tracking.ogtitle: What is Email open tracking? | Ciphera

proof-of-work.title: What is Proof-of-work challenge? - Glossary | Ciphera
proof-of-work.description: A proof-of-work challenge requires a client to perform a small, verifiable computation before a request is accepted — cheap for one user, expensive enough at scale to make bulk automated abuse uneconomical.

bot-detection.title: What is Bot detection? - Glossary | Ciphera
bot-detection.description: Bot detection distinguishes automated traffic from genuine human visitors before allowing an action — form submission, login, checkout — to prevent spam, credential stuffing, and scraping at scale.

honeypot.title: What is Honeypot? - Glossary | Ciphera
honeypot.description: A honeypot, in bot detection, is a form field hidden from human view but present in the page’s HTML — automated submitters that fill in every field reveal themselves, while real visitors never see it to fill in.

gdpr.title: What is GDPR? - Glossary | Ciphera
gdpr.description: The GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation, EU 2016/679) is the European Union’s data protection law, in force since 25 May 2018, governing how personal data of people in the EU/EEA is collected, processed, and transferred.

fadp.title: What is FADP / nFADP? - Glossary | Ciphera
fadp.description: The FADP (Federal Act on Data Protection) is Switzerland’s national data protection law; its fully revised version (nFADP) took effect 1 September 2023, modernizing Swiss law to align closely — though not identically — with the GDPR.

eprivacy-directive.title: What is ePrivacy Directive? - Glossary | Ciphera
eprivacy-directive.description: The ePrivacy Directive (2002/58/EC, amended 2009) is the EU law governing confidentiality of electronic communications, including the cookie-consent rule: storing or reading anything on a user’s device requires prior consent unless it is strictly necessary.

consent-banner.title: What is Consent banner? - Glossary | Ciphera
consent-banner.description: A consent banner is the on-page prompt asking a visitor to accept or decline non-essential cookies and tracking, required under the EU ePrivacy Directive whenever a site stores or reads anything on the visitor’s device that isn’t strictly necessary.

data-processing-agreement.title: What is DPA (data processing agreement)? - Glossary | Ciphera
data-processing-agreement.description: A data processing agreement (DPA) is the contract required by GDPR Article 28 between a data controller and a data processor, setting out the scope, purpose, and security obligations governing the processor’s handling of personal data on the controller’s behalf.
data-processing-agreement.ogtitle: What is DPA (data processing agreement)? | Ciphera

sub-processor.title: What is Sub-processor? - Glossary | Ciphera
sub-processor.description: A sub-processor is a third party a data processor engages to help process personal data on a controller’s behalf — a cloud host, for example. GDPR requires the controller’s prior authorization and a flow-down contract.

standard-contractual-clauses.title: What is SCCs (standard contractual clauses)? - Glossary | Ciphera
standard-contractual-clauses.description: Standard contractual clauses (SCCs) are European Commission-approved contract templates that legalize personal-data transfers from the EU/EEA to countries without an adequacy decision by extending GDPR-equivalent protections.
standard-contractual-clauses.ogtitle: What is SCCs (standard contractual clauses)? | Ciphera

eu-us-data-privacy-framework.title: What is EU-US Data Privacy Framework? - Glossary | Ciphera
eu-us-data-privacy-framework.description: The EU-US Data Privacy Framework (DPF) is a 2023 adequacy decision permitting personal-data transfers to US companies that self-certify to its principles — successor to the invalidated Privacy Shield and Safe Harbor.
eu-us-data-privacy-framework.ogtitle: What is EU-US Data Privacy Framework? | Ciphera

data-residency.title: What is Data residency? - Glossary | Ciphera
data-residency.description: Data residency is the physical or jurisdictional location where an organization’s data is stored — a deliberate infrastructure choice, distinct from data sovereignty, which concerns whose laws govern that data regardless of where it sits.

data-sovereignty.title: What is Data sovereignty? - Glossary | Ciphera
data-sovereignty.description: Data sovereignty is the principle that data is subject to the laws of the jurisdiction that governs it — broader than data residency, since a legal claim can reach across borders regardless of where servers physically sit.

privacy-by-design.title: What is Privacy by design? - Glossary | Ciphera
privacy-by-design.description: Privacy by design is the principle — codified as a legal obligation in GDPR Article 25 — that data protection must be built into a system’s architecture from the outset, not added afterward as a policy or a configuration toggle.
privacy-by-design.ogtitle: What is Privacy by design? | Ciphera

data-controller.title: What is Data controller? - Glossary | Ciphera
data-controller.description: A data controller is the natural or legal person that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data — under GDPR, the controller bears primary responsibility for lawful processing and for honoring data subjects’ rights.

data-processor.title: What is Data processor? - Glossary | Ciphera
data-processor.description: A data processor is the natural or legal person that processes personal data on behalf of, and under the instructions of, a data controller — without independently deciding why or how that data is used.

personal-data.title: What is Personal data? - Glossary | Ciphera
personal-data.description: Personal data, under GDPR, is any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person — a deliberately broad definition covering not just names and IDs but anything that can be linked back to someone, directly or in combination with other data.

pseudonymization.title: What is Pseudonymization? - Glossary | Ciphera
pseudonymization.description: Pseudonymization is processing personal data so it can no longer be attributed to a specific person without additional information, which is kept separately and secured — a GDPR-recognized risk-reduction measure, but the data remains personal data in scope.

anonymization.title: What is Anonymization? - Glossary | Ciphera
anonymization.description: Anonymization is processing data such that the individual it once related to can no longer be identified by any means reasonably likely to be used — done correctly, the result falls entirely outside GDPR’s scope, unlike pseudonymized data.

warrant-canary.title: What is Warrant canary? - Glossary | Ciphera
warrant-canary.description: A warrant canary is a regularly published statement that an organization has not received a secret government order — its disappearance warns users implicitly, since a gag order would forbid saying so directly.
